# Files, CSV and JSON


<!-- WARNING: THIS FILE WAS AUTOGENERATED! DO NOT EDIT! -->

Read text with `•nget`, parse it with `•csv` or `•json`, and calculate.
`•csv⁻` and `•json⁻` produce text, which `•nput` writes to a file.

``` text
sales←•csv •nget "sales.csv"
totals←+/¨sales
"totals.json" •nput •json⁻ totals
```

Options go on the left as a keyed vector, and the data goes on the
right. Option names are case-insensitive.

## Files

``` bpl
]help •nget
```

# `•nget` — Read a file

`•nget path` reads a UTF-8 text file. `•nget "-"` reads the rest of
standard input. A path that starts with `./` or `../` is relative to the
file holding the code, as for [`•load`](system/load.qmd).

`X •nget path` takes an options record on the left: `binary` (`1` reads
a vector of byte values, as in `["binary":1] •nget path`) and `encoding`
(`"UTF-8"`, the only encoding). [Files](data.ipynb#files) covers bytes
and options.

Errors: `IO` for missing files, invalid UTF-8, other file errors, and
standard input that fails or that the frontend doesn’t provide; `DOMAIN`
for invalid options.

``` bpl
]help •nput
```

# `•nput` — Write a file

`path •nput data` writes `data` to a new file. It returns the number of
bytes written as a [shy](terms.qmd#term-shy) result. Text is written as
UTF-8. An array of numbers is written as bytes, each from 0 to 255, in
ravel order. A path that starts with `./` or `../` is relative to the
file holding the code, as for [`•load`](system/load.qmd).

`"-" •nput data` writes `data` to standard output, with no line ending
added. Text written this way just before a read of `⎕` is that read’s
prompt. See [`⎕`](glyphs/quad.qmd#input).

`X •nput data` takes an options record on the left: `path`, `overwrite`
(`1` replaces an existing file, as in
`["path":p "overwrite":1] •nput data`) and `encoding` (`"UTF-8"`, for
text). With the option `unique`, `•nput` writes a new file with a unique
name inside the directory `path`. It returns the new file’s path, which
is displayed. The option `prefix` sets the start of the name, as for
[`•mkdir`](system/mkdir.qmd). Plain text on the left is the path.
[Files](data.ipynb#files) covers bytes and options.

Errors: `IO` for an existing file without `overwrite`, and for other
file errors; `DOMAIN` for invalid options or byte values, and for bytes
written to standard output that aren’t UTF-8.

``` bpl
text←•nget "sales.csv"
"copy.csv" •nput text
["path":"copy.csv" "overwrite":1] •nput text
```

The parent directory must already exist when `•nput` writes a file. With
`"binary":1`, `•nget` returns exact integers in `0…255`. `•nput` writes
an array of whole numbers in `0…255` as bytes. It checks the data before
opening the file.

``` bpl
bytes←["binary":1] •nget "image.bin"
"copy.bin" •nput bytes
"UTF-8" •ucs bytes           ⍝ decode UTF-8 when appropriate
bytes-256ₓ×bytes≥128ₓ         ⍝ signed-byte interpretation
```

## Numeric input

``` bpl
]help •vfi
```

# `•vfi` — Numeric input

`•vfi text` returns two vectors, `[valid numbers]`, with a flag and a
value for each whitespace-separated field of `text`. An invalid field
has the flag `0ₓ` and the value zero. The zero is converted to the other
values’ type, as a reader’s `fill` is: `•vfi "2ₓ nope"` gives
`[[1 0]ₓ;[2 0]ₓ]`. Fields are parsed as numbers, never executed.

A field can be any of BPL’s written forms of a number, with plain
letters or subscripts. `•vfi` reads back the numbers that `⍕` displays:

``` bpl
•vfi ⍕1r3 1j2 1e20   ⍝ [[1 1 1]ₓ [1ᵣ3 1ⱼ2 1ₑ20]]
```

`separators •vfi text` splits on each character in `separators` instead.
It trims whitespace around fields. An empty field is a valid `0`.
[Numeric input](data.ipynb#numeric-input) covers it.

Errors: `DOMAIN` when either argument is not text.

Invalid fields have flag `0ₓ` and value `0`. Valid fields have flag
`1ₓ`:

``` bpl
[valid nums]←•vfi "12 nope -3 1.5"
valid
nums
valid#nums
```

    [1 0 1 1]ₓ

    12 0 ¯3 1.5

    12 ¯3 1.5

A number written plainly, such as `2` or `1.5`, is approximate. A number
written with an `x` suffix, such as `3x`, or as a rational, such as
`1r4`, is exact. `•vfi` also accepts the subscript forms that `⍕`
displays, such as `1ᵣ4` and `1ₑ20`, complex numbers written with `j` or
`J`, `∞`, `inf`, `infinity`, ASCII signs and signed exponents. `•vfi`
converts `nan` to `$n`.

If any number is approximate and every number can be represented exactly
as a float, all the numbers become approximate. Otherwise each number
keeps its kind. The `0` from an invalid field doesn’t count as
approximate.

``` bpl
1⊃•vfi "2 3x 1r4 1j-2 -1e-3 ∞"
```

    2 3 0.25 1ⱼ¯2 ¯0.001 ∞

`separators •vfi text` splits `text` on any character in `separators`
and trims surrounding whitespace from each field. Empty fields are valid
and have value `0`. Internal whitespace remains part of the field.

``` bpl
',' •vfi "3.9,2.4,,76,"
'◇' •vfi "1 ◇ 2 3 ◇ 4"
```

    (1ₓ 1ₓ 1ₓ 1ₓ 1ₓ◇3.9 2.4 0 76 0)

    (1ₓ 0ₓ 1ₓ◇1 0 4)

For empty input, `•vfi` returns two empty vectors. When `separators` is
`""`, nonempty `text` is one field. A DOMAIN error occurs if either
argument is not character text.

## JSON

``` bpl
]help •json
```

# `•json` — JSON

`•json text` reads JSON5, which includes all JSON. JSON5 adds comments,
trailing commas, single-quoted strings, unquoted keys, hexadecimal
numbers, `Infinity` and `NaN`. Objects become keyed vectors. Arrays
become vectors. Strings become character vectors. An integer outside the
64-bit range is read as its nearest float: `9223372036854775808` becomes
`9.223372037ₑ18`. `true` and `false` become `$t` and `$f`.

`•json⁻ Y` writes JSON text. Keyed axes become objects. Unkeyed axes
become arrays. Character vectors become strings. Keyed entries that hold
functions are left out. NaN is written as `null`.

`["fill":v] •json text` reads `null` as `v`. The fill is converted to
its array’s type if the conversion preserves its value:
`["fill":0] •json "[1,null,3]"` gives `[1 0 3]ₓ`, and
`["fill":0] •json "[true,null]"` gives `$t $f`. If the conversion would
change the fill’s value, as with the default NaN beside integers, the
array is read as floats. `["fill":v] •json⁻ Y` writes `v` as `null`.
[JSON](data.ipynb#json) covers the conversions.

Under [static kinds](numbers.qmd#static-kinds), an array of integers is
read at the [`int`](system/prefs.qmd) width, and a value that doesn’t
fit raises a `DOMAIN` error. `["types":R] •json text` sets the type of
the arrays in named fields: `R` maps a field’s name to a number of that
type, as `•csv`’s `types` option does, and every array in a field of
that name is read as that type:

``` bpl
•prefs ["kinds":"static"]
(["types":["id":0ₓ₈]] •json "{""id"":[3000000000,7],""n"":[1,2]}").id    ⍝ [3000000000 7]ₓ₈
•prefs ["kinds":"dynamic"]
```

Errors: `DOMAIN` for malformed JSON, with its line and column, and for
values that JSON can’t hold: an infinity that isn’t `fill`, out-of-range
floats, rationals that aren’t whole, complex numbers and other
functions. Also `DOMAIN` for a value that can’t be converted to its
array’s type unchanged, and for a `types` entry that names no field
holding an array.

Nested structure is kept:

``` bpl
person←•json "{""name"":""Ann"",""scores"":[10,20]}"
person.name
person.scores
```

    "Ann"

    [10 20]ₓ

`•json` also reads JSON5, with comments, trailing commas, single-quoted
strings and unquoted keys.

``` bpl
•json "{name: 'Ann', scores: [10, 20,]}  // JSON5"
```

    ["name":"Ann" "scores":[10 20]ₓ]

`"f.json" •nput •json⁻ Y` writes JSON to a file. `•json⁻` exports the
contents of a scalar array. Axis names and empty-array
[prototypes](terms.qmd#term-prototype) are left out:

``` bpl
•json⁻ ["name":"Ann" "scores":[10 20]ₓ]
•json⁻ [1 2◇3 4]ₓ
•json⁻ •json "{}"
```

    "{""name"":""Ann"",""scores"":[10,20]}"

    "[[1,2],[3,4]]"

    "{}"

JSON integers are exact when they fit in 64 bits. A larger one is read
as its nearest float, because only `ᵣ` makes unbounded integers. Numbers
with a decimal point or an exponent are approximate. Numbers in a JSON
array combine by the rule in [Numeric input](#numeric-input). `true` and
`false` are read as `$t` and `$f`. `•json⁻` writes Booleans back as
`true` and `false`:

``` bpl
•json "[9223372036854775809,1.5,true,false]"
•json⁻ •json "[true,false]"
```

    9.223372037ₑ18 1.5 1 0

    "[true,false]"

`fill` replaces `null` on import. The fill value is converted to the
array’s type if that conversion preserves its value, as it does for `¯1`
here. Because the default `fill` is NaN, an integer array containing
`null` is read as floats. On export, NaN and the `fill` value become
`null`:

``` bpl
•json "[1,null,3]"
["fill":¯1] •json "[1,null,3]"
["fill":∞] •json⁻ 1ₓ ∞ 3ₓ
```

    1 $n 3

    [1 ¯1 3]ₓ

    "[1,null,3]"

For duplicate object members, `•json` keeps the last value.

## CSV

``` bpl
]help •csv
```

# `•csv` — CSV

`•csv text` parses CSV into a vector of columns. Headers become keys.
Numeric columns become numbers. An integer outside the 64-bit range is
read as its nearest float. Missing numeric cells become the `fill`
option’s value, NaN by default. Missing text cells become `""`.

`ifill` replaces missing cells in integer columns without replacing NaNs
in float columns. It must be a whole real number. It applies to inferred
integer columns and to integer columns requested by `types`, not to
Boolean or float columns.

`fills` overrides individual columns, as a record keyed by column name
or a vector with one value per column. Its values must be numeric for
numeric columns and text for text columns. The precedence is `fills`,
then `ifill` for integer columns, then `fill` for numeric columns or
`""` for text.

A fill is converted to its column’s inferred type when that type can
hold its value exactly. With `ifill` set to `0`, a missing integer is
read as `0ₓ`. NaN or `0.5` from `fill` or `fills` instead makes an
inferred integer column floating-point. A column whose cells are all
missing is text unless `types` gives it a numeric type.

Under [static kinds](numbers.qmd#static-kinds), every integer column is
read at the `int` width whatever its values, as every new integer is. A
value that doesn’t fit raises a `DOMAIN` error that names the column.

The `types` option sets each column’s type, given as a value of that
type. A number, such as `0ₓ₈`, `0ₚ` or `$f`, makes a numeric column of
its type. That type must hold each of the column’s values exactly, and
the fill at its missing cells, or `•csv` raises a `DOMAIN` error. With a
float type, values are rounded to its width. With text, such as `""`,
the column is read as written: `02134` stays `"02134"`. A record sets
the columns that it names. A vector sets every column in order, and
needs one value for each column. A file with no header needs a vector:

``` bpl
•prefs ["kinds":"static"]
t←"id,price,flag,zip",(•ucs 10),"3000000000,1.5,1,02134",(•ucs 10),"7,2.25,0,10001"
T←["types":["id":0ₓ₈ "price":0ₚ "flag":$f "zip":""]] •csv t
T.id                       ⍝ [3000000000 7]ₓ₈
T.flag                     ⍝ $t $f
(•storage T.price).kind    ⍝ "float64"
T.zip                      ⍝ "02134" "10001"
•prefs ["kinds":"dynamic"]
["header":$f "types":["" 0ₓ]] •csv "a,12",(•ucs 10),"b,7"   ⍝ [["a" "b"] [12 7]ₓ]
```

`•csv⁻ T` writes CSV text for a vector of columns. Keys supply the
header. Column lengths must agree. NaN and the selected fill for each
column are written as empty cells. `fills`, `ifill` and `fill` have the
same precedence as on import.

`•csv` and `•csv⁻` both take options on the left: `header`, `separator`,
`quote`, `doublequote`, `escapechar`, `decimal`, `thousands`, `trim`,
`fill`, `ifill` and `fills`. `•csv` also takes `missing` and `types`,
and `•csv⁻` takes `forcequotes` and `eol`. `"forcequotes":2` quotes
every field. [CSV](data.ipynb#csv) describes the options.

Errors: `DOMAIN` for invalid options, duplicate headers, incompatible
fills, and cells that CSV can’t hold: rationals that aren’t whole,
complex numbers, functions or nested cells, and for a value that doesn’t
keep itself in its column’s type; `LENGTH` for unequal record widths or
columns, or a `types` or `fills` vector of the wrong length.

Each numeric column uses compact integer or float storage where
possible:

``` bpl
text←"price,qty
10.5,2
20.0,4"
T←•csv text
T
T.qty
+/¨T
```

    ["price":[10.5 20] "qty":[2 4]ₓ]

    [2 4]ₓ

    ["price":30.5 "qty":6ₓ]

`"f.csv" •nput •csv⁻ T` writes CSV to a file. When `T` has no keys,
`•csv⁻` writes the data without a header row. Parsing the text restores
the columns:

``` bpl
T←["price":10.5 20;"qty":2ₓ 4ₓ]
•csv •csv⁻ T
```

    ["price":[10.5 20] "qty":[2 4]ₓ]

### CSV options

``` bpl
text←"price;qty
10,5;2
20,0;4"
opts←["separator":';' "decimal":',']
T←opts •csv text
T
csv←opts •csv⁻ T
opts •csv csv
```

    ["price":[10.5 20] "qty":[2 4]ₓ]

    ["price":[10.5 20] "qty":[2 4]ₓ]

T.id

`separator`, `quote` and `escapechar` must be distinct ASCII characters
other than CR, LF or NUL. Fields may contain Unicode characters, doubled
quotes and embedded newlines. `•csv` accepts LF, CRLF and CR record
endings. When `escapechar` is set, `•csv⁻` quotes every field and
doubles each literal escape character. When `quote` is `""`, `•csv⁻`
gives DOMAIN for a field that requires quoting.

### Numbers and missing cells

To infer a column’s type, `•csv` examines the whole column, ignoring
missing cells. Integer fields produce exact numbers. Decimal and
scientific notation produce floats. A column containing other text stays
text. Quoted numbers are also used to infer the column’s type.

``` bpl
T←•csv "count,label
2,001
3,yes"
T.count
T.label
```

    [2 3]ₓ

    "001" "yes"

A column of integers uses integer storage when every value fits in 64
bits. A larger integer is read as its nearest float. A value with a
decimal point or an exponent is approximate. A column’s numbers combine
by the rule in [Numeric input](#numeric-input).

By default, missing numeric cells become NaN, written `$n`. Because NaN
is a float, an integer column with a missing cell becomes floats. If
that column also holds an integer too large for a float to represent
exactly, each item keeps its kind in [mixed
storage](terms.qmd#term-mixed-storage). Missing text cells become `""`.
A column whose cells are all missing is read as text unless `types`
gives it a numeric type.

``` bpl
T←•csv "price,qty
10.5,2
,4"
T.price
T.qty
```

    10.5 $n

    [2 4]ₓ

Use `missing` to add missing-cell strings and `fill` to replace missing
numeric cells:

``` bpl
text←"qty
NA
4"
["missing":"NA" "fill":¯1] •csv text
```

    ["qty":[¯1 4]ₓ]

Use `ifill` to keep missing integer counts as integers without replacing
NaNs in float columns. `fills` overrides individual columns. Here IDs
use `¯1`, quantities use `0`, prices keep NaN, and labels use
`"unknown"`:

``` bpl
text←"id,qty,price,label
7,3,1.5,known
,,,"
opts←["ifill":0 "fills":["id":¯1 "label":"unknown"]]
T←opts •csv text
T
opts •csv⁻ T
```

    ["id":[7 ¯1]ₓ "qty":[3 0]ₓ "price":[1.5 $n] "label":["known" "unknown"]]

    "id,qty,price,label
    7,3,1.5,known
    ,,,
    "

`•csv⁻` writes negative numbers with `-`, floats in decimal or
scientific notation, and exact integers plainly. It writes infinity as
`inf` or `-inf`. NaN and each column’s selected fill are written as
empty cells, using the same `fills`, `ifill`, `fill` precedence as on
import. It gives DOMAIN for rationals that aren’t whole, complex
numbers, functions and nested nonstring cells.

For empty input, `•csv` returns an empty unkeyed vector. For header-only
input, it returns keyed empty columns. Empty header names are allowed.
Duplicate header names give DOMAIN. `•csv` gives LENGTH for unequal
record widths, and `•csv⁻` gives LENGTH for unequal column lengths. When
`types` gives a column a numeric type and a cell is not a number, the
DOMAIN error reports the cell’s row and column.

## Repeated text

When text is repeated in `•csv`, `•json` or Python data, all cells
containing that text share the same array. This sharing applies to the
first 65,536 distinct texts in each `•csv` column, `•json` document and
Python conversion. A long column of repeated text then takes less
memory, and `=`, `∪`, `⍷` and `⌸` compare only the distinct arrays.

For text created in BPL, such as words produced by splitting a string,
each cell stores a separate array. Selecting each word from the distinct
words makes cells containing the same word share an array:

``` bpl
words←' ' ≠⊆⊢ "to be or not to be"
u←∪words
words←[uιwords]⌷u
words
```

    "to" "be" "or" "not" "to" "be"
